summary: For ages 8–9: multiply and divide mentally using place value, known and derived facts, including the special cases ×0, ×1 and ÷1, and multiplying three numbers by choosing a useful pair first. The goal is flexible strategy choice — looking for the easy route before calculating — with the identity/zero cases understood through the equal-groups meaning rather than memorised as rules. Note: ÷0 is out of scope and is undefined; keep to ×0, ×1, ÷1.
misconceptions: Thinking ×0 gives the other number, or ×1 doubles/changes it, when treated as rote rules.
Believing multiplication always makes a number bigger (so ×1 or later × a fraction surprises).
Not reordering three factors, so multiplying left-to-right the hard way.
Miscounting place value in 40×6 (getting 24 instead of 240).

activities.title: Reorder three factors to find the easy pair
steps: Work out 2 × 7 × 5 in your head, saying aloud which two numbers you multiply first and why.
Try pairing 2 and 5 first to make 10, then multiply by 7 to get 70; compare this with going left to right (2 × 7 = 14, then × 5 = 70).
Check that different orders give the same total: is 2 × 7 × 5 the same as 5 × 2 × 7? Explain why you are allowed to reorder.
Repeat with 2 × 9 × 5 and 4 × 3 × 5, each time scanning for a pair that makes a ten or a known fact first.
activities.insight: Reordering factors is always allowed (commutativity/associativity) and the total stays the same — but some orderings turn a fiddly three-number product into a single known fact, so it pays to look for the friendly pair before calculating.

activities.title: Understand ×1, ×0 and ÷1 through groups
steps: Lay out counters to show 8 × 1 as 'one group of 8' and '8 groups of 1'; confirm both give 8.
Show 8 × 0 as '8 groups of nothing' — every group is empty, so the total is 0.
Show 8 ÷ 1 as one whole group of 8 (or sharing 8 into groups of one) and confirm the result is still 8.
Say in your own words why n × 1 = n, why n × 0 = 0, and why n ÷ 1 = n.
Contrast 8 × 0 with 8 + 0: adding 0 leaves 8, but 0 groups of 8 (or 8 groups of 0) is nothing — notice the roles are different.
activities.insight: ×1 and ÷1 leave a number unchanged because you have one whole group (or share into groups of one), and ×0 gives 0 because there are no groups (or every group is empty) — these are meanings to be seen, not rules to memorise.

activities.title: Scale with place value for multiples of ten
steps: Work out 40 × 6 mentally by reasoning '4 tens × 6 = 24 tens = 240'; say the 'tens' name aloud as you go.
Explain how knowing 4 × 6 = 24 helps you get 40 × 6.
Try 30 × 7 and 50 × 8 the same way, keeping the place-value name attached to each digit.
Check your answer is sensible: 40 × 6 is exactly ten times 4 × 6, so 240, not 24.
activities.insight: A known fact can be scaled by place value: 40 × 6 is ten times 4 × 6, so the answer is 240, not 24 — keeping the 'tens' label attached prevents losing the place value.

activities.title: Consolidate and check reasoning
steps: Decide which pair you would multiply first in 2 × 9 × 5 and say why.
Give the results for 7 × 0, 7 × 1 and 7 ÷ 1, and explain each using the groups meaning.
Answer: why does any number × 1 equal that same number?
Explain why you are free to reorder the factors in a three-number product.
activities.insight: Strategy choice and the special-case results are things you can state and justify, not just compute — being able to explain why confirms genuine understanding.

checkQuestion: Ask the child to do these in their head, saying how: 40 × 6; then 2 × 7 × 5 (watch whether they reorder to pair 2 and 5); and slip in 8 × 0 and 8 × 1. Watch the place-value reasoning, the choice of a useful pair, and how they treat the ×0 and ×1 cases.
checkAnswer: 240 (4×6 = 24, then ×10 for the tens); 70 (reorder to 2×5 = 10, ×7 = 70); 8×0 = 0; 8×1 = 8. The teacher watches for place-value scaling, using commutativity/associativity to pick an easy pair, and correct, reasoned handling of the identity/zero cases.
